terms.meaning: the markup language that describes the structure of a web page.
a group of input fields that a user fills in and submits.
a file that controls how the page looks, here styles.css.
a layer placed on top of the page to block interaction while work runs.

sections.name: File setup (part 1)
sections.title: Page header and tab bar
sections.what: Sets up the page title, the header banner, and five tab buttons that switch between sections.
sections.why: Likely reason: gives the user a clear way to move between tools on one page.
sections.watch_out: Each button calls a named function in app.js, so renaming those functions breaks navigation.

sections.name: File setup (part 2)
sections.title: Survey planner form
sections.what: Provides fields for the research goal, audience, required topics and model type, plus the button that sends the request and the results area.
sections.why: Likely reason: collects everything the planner handler reads.
sections.watch_out: Field names such as goal and audience are read by name in app.js, so renaming them breaks the planner.

sections.name: File setup (part 3)
sections.title: Question author form
sections.what: Provides a topic field, a question type list, a count field, and the results area for the author tab.
sections.why: Likely reason: collects the inputs the author handler reads.
sections.watch_out: The question type list values such as NPS and MaxDiff are sent to the backend, so they must match what it accepts.

sections.name: File setup (part 4)
sections.title: Survey validator form and results
sections.what: Provides a large text box for pasting survey JSON and a button that runs the check, plus the results area.
sections.why: Likely reason: the validator needs the full survey pasted as text.
sections.watch_out: The text box is required, but invalid JSON is only caught after the button is pressed.

sections.name: File setup (part 5)
sections.title: Model browser and document upload
sections.what: Provides task and type dropdowns with a refresh button for models, and a document type, audience, file picker, upload button and document list for the upload tab.
sections.why: Likely reason: these controls feed the model filter and the upload handler.
sections.watch_out: The upload audience label points at the planner audience field, which is a labelling bug.

sections.name: File setup (part 6)
sections.title: Footer and loading overlay
sections.what: Shows the backend status badge, a link to the API documentation, a full-screen spinner, and loads the script file.
sections.why: Likely reason: the status badge and spinner are updated by app.js. The script is placed last so the page is ready first.
sections.watch_out: The status badge id must stay the same because app.js looks it up by that name.

summary: The main web page for the classic version of the research tool, with five tabs for planning, authoring, validating, browsing models and uploading documents.
purpose: Gives the user the forms, buttons and output areas that app.js and styles.css work with.
why: Likely reason: a single static page keeps the tool simple to run. Reason not stated in the code.
how: The page loads the stylesheet in the head, builds a header, a tab bar, five tab sections with their forms, and a footer showing backend status. A loading overlay sits at the end. The script file is loaded last so the page exists before the script runs.
inputs: User typing, selections, and file choices in the forms.
outputs: Calls the handler functions in app.js when forms are submitted or buttons are clicked.
risks: Two different controls share the audience name, and the upload form label points to the wrong control, which can confuse screen readers and form submission. The backend link is fixed to localhost.
debug: If a button does nothing, check that its handler name matches a function in app.js. If styling is missing, confirm styles.css loads.
